Magnetic and electric surface currents are induced at the inner boundary of a cylindrical invisibility cloak by incoming electromagnetic waves.
These surface currents have no counterparts in the coordinate transformation theory.
Electromagnetic fields can penetrate into the concealed region under specified conditions but carry no power.
The field distribution inside the cloak can be unsymmetrical when a circularly polarized wave is obliquely incident.
The far-field scattering for a nonideal cylindrical cloak increases with material loss.
The cloak layer is an anisotropic and inhomogeneous medium with specific permittivity and permeability tensors.
The ideal cloak parameters satisfy ε_φ/ε_r = μ_φ/μ_r = (r-R_1)/(r), where R_1 and R_2 are inner and outer radii.
The cloak achieves perfect invisibility for both normal and oblique incidence of plane waves.
Discontinuities of tangential electric and magnetic fields at the inner boundary induce surface currents.
Extending the inner boundary inward distributes the surface current over a finite region rather than concentrating it at a boundary.
No electromagnetic power penetrates into the concealed region even when fields do.
The cloak must be infinitely long along the cylinder axis to fully shield a 3D object.
Increasing loss tangent from 0.001 to 1 increases scattering and shifts the angle of minimum scattering.
The tangential Poynting power at the inner boundary of a cylindrical cloak is not zero, unlike in spherical cloaks.
The cloak's response is analyzed using full-wave scattering theory and cylindrical wave expansions.
The induced surface currents act like a perfect magnetic conductor at the inner boundary.
The cloak's invisibility is sensitive to mismatches in constitutive parameters.
The cloak's field distribution inside is asymmetric for oblique circularly polarized incidence.
The scattering coefficients converge slowly for the zeroth order mode due to surface currents.
The cloak's design is based on coordinate transformation of empty space into a shell surrounding the object.
